925.title: Tulsidas bows to the whole world
925.hook: Tulsidas opens his Ramayana bowing to the saints, the wicked, and a world full of Sita and Ram
925.carry: the whole world is full of Sita and Ram
925.tomorrow: why does the Hanuman Chalisa start with a mirror?
925.howItsDone: Readers of the Ramcharitmanas begin with its opening invocations, and the line about the whole world being full of Sita and Ram is often recited on its own with folded hands.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tulsidas bowed to Vani and Vinayaka at the door of the Ramcharitmanas, and wrote for his own heart's joy.
screen: `TULSIDAS.` · `FOR MY OWN HEART'S JOY.`

segments.voice: Speeches at a wedding usually go the same way. Thank the parents. Thank the friends who flew in. Thank the cooks. Tulsidas, at the door of his great poem, does something like that, but stranger. He bows to his teacher. He bows to the saints. And then, with what sounds like a straight face, he bows to the wicked, the people who wish others harm. He means it. And the reason he gives is the lesson.
screen: `HE BOWS TO THE TEACHER.` → `HE BOWS TO THE SAINTS.` → `THEN HE BOWS TO THE WICKED.`

segments.voice: The opening of the Ramcharitmanas is a long series of bows. First the teacher. Then the saints, and here Tulsidas has a lovely picture. He calls the company of good people a pilgrimage that walks: like Prayag, which the poem calls the king of pilgrimage places, but moving about the world on its own feet. It comes down your street. Then he bows to the wicked, sincerely, he says: people glad at another's loss and sad at another's gain. Why bow to them? He doesn't pretend they're good. Part of it is a poet's humility: he asks even the hostile reader to be kind to the poem. The deeper reason is a picture of the world. Tulsidas says the maker made this world a mixture, the living and the lifeless, good qualities and faults, all woven together. And the saint is like the swan in the old story, that can take the milk out of milk mixed with water, and leave the water behind. Good and bad come mixed, sometimes inside the same person. The work is to take the milk. Knowing the whole world to be full of Sita and Ram, Tulsidas says, he bows to it all with joined palms. That's the teaching, one of Hinduism's biggest: God isn't only in the temple. The whole world is full of Sita and Ram, so a devotee greets all of it with joined palms. Many Hindus explain namaste the same way: the palms meet because God is there in the other person too.
screen: `A PILGRIMAGE THAT WALKS.` · `A BOW TO THE WICKED.` · `THE SWAN TAKES THE MILK.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD FULL OF SITA AND RAM.`

segments.voice: Bring your palms together at your chest, or just rest your hands, and bring to mind three people: someone good to you, someone you hardly notice, someone you find difficult. For each, without changing your opinion, look for the milk in the mixture, one small good thing that's really there. Let a quiet bow go toward each of them, and if you pray, say Sita Ram softly for each, the greeting many Ram devotees use.
Tulsidas. The poet who bowed to the saints, the wicked, and a whole world full of Sita and Ram.
screen: `TULSIDAS — today's word`.

926.title: The Hanuman Chalisa
926.hook: the hymn many Hindus know by heart begins with a mirror and ends at Ram's door
926.carry: dasya: Hanuman's strength is for serving Ram
926.tomorrow: why did a teacher tell a singer to stop whining?
926.howItsDone: Devotees of Hanuman recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often from memory, at home and in temples, and some make a point of saying it on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tulsidas bowed to the saints, to the wicked, and to the whole world as full of Sita and Ram.
screen: `TULSIDAS.` · `THE WHOLE WORLD FULL OF SITA AND RAM.`

segments.voice: A truck driver in traffic, murmuring under his breath. A student outside an exam hall, lips moving. A grandmother on a Tuesday evening, a small book open on her lap that she doesn't need, because she knows every word. They could all be saying the same thing: a hymn to Hanuman, short enough to say in a few minutes, steady enough to lean on. Tradition gives it to Tulsidas, and the hymn signs his name near its end.
screen: `MURMURED IN TRAFFIC.` → `KNOWN BY HEART.` → `THE HANUMAN CHALISA.`

segments.voice: The Hanuman Chalisa doesn't start with Hanuman. It starts with a mirror. The first couplet says, roughly: with the dust from my teacher's lotus feet I polish the mirror of my mind, and then I sing the pure fame of Ram. Before praising anyone, clean the glass, so what you see isn't smudged by you. The second couplet is even more honest. Knowing myself to be without understanding, it says, I remember Hanuman, son of the wind. Give me strength, wisdom and knowledge, and take away my troubles. That's the posture of the whole hymn. Not I am strong, but I'm not wise enough, so I'm calling on the one who is. Then the verses praise Hanuman piece by piece: his strength, his leap across the sea, the healing herb that revived Lakshman. But one line says what all that strength is for. Hanuman is the guard at Ram's door. All that power, used for service, near Ram, doing what's needed. Near the end, the poet steps forward with his own name. Tulsidas, the hymn says, is forever Hari's servant, and he asks the Lord to make a home in his heart. So the poet ends where Hanuman stands: a servant. Bhakti has a name for this love: dasya, the love of a servant for the Lord, and Hanuman is its great example. It's why many Hindus say the Chalisa before an exam, a journey, a hard night: not as a lucky charm, but to clean the mirror, ask for strength, wisdom and knowledge, and use them the way Hanuman did, for someone else.
screen: `POLISH THE MIRROR OF THE MIND.` · `WITHOUT UNDERSTANDING, I REMEMBER.` · `THE GUARD AT RAM'S DOOR.` · then, large: `DASYA: THE SERVANT'S LOVE.`

segments.voice: Picture your mind as a glass with the day's smudges on it, a worry, a grudge, a hurry, and with each breath out, let one smudge soften. Then, if it feels honest, admit one thing you don't understand right now, and ask quietly for the strength to serve anyway. If you pray, you can turn that asking to God, or to Hanuman, in whatever words you already use.
Tulsidas. The poet of Ram, to whom tradition gives the Hanuman Chalisa, a servant's hymn.

927.title: Surdas sings the child Krishna
927.hook: a singer by the river stops singing about himself
927.carry: vatsalya: loving God as your own child
927.tomorrow: what does a boy with butter on his face tell his mother?
927.howItsDone: Songs from the Sursagar are sung in Krishna temples and homes in north India, and in the Pushti Marg tradition founded by Vallabhacharya they are part of the daily service before Krishna's image.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tulsidas and the Hanuman Chalisa, which polishes the mirror of the mind. Dasya: Hanuman's strength is for serving Ram.
screen: `THE HANUMAN CHALISA.` · `DASYA: STRENGTH THAT SERVES.`

segments.voice: A singer sits near a river and sings about himself. How low he has fallen. How far he is from God. How little he deserves. That's how one old account remembers Surdas before his life turned. Tradition says he was blind, and lived beside the Yamuna, in the country of Braj, where Krishna grew up. One day a teacher named Vallabhacharya stops to listen. He hears the sad songs through. Then he says one thing, and it changes what Surdas sings from then on.
screen: `A SINGER BY THE RIVER.` → `SONGS ABOUT HIS OWN FAILINGS.` → `A TEACHER STOPS TO LISTEN.`

segments.voice: The account comes from a book of stories about Vallabha's followers. The teacher says, roughly: why whine like this? Sing about the Lord's play, his lila. And Surdas does. He turns from his own sorrow to a child's life in a cowherd village. The songs carried under his name are called the Sursagar, the ocean of Sur, full of small household things: a cradle, a churn of yogurt, a mother calling her boy in to eat. Here's one. Little Krishna comes to Yashoda with a complaint. Mother, when will my braid grow? You keep telling me to drink my milk and it'll get long and thick like my brother Balarama's. I've drunk and drunk, and it's still short. A tiny boy comparing hair with his big brother, suspecting his mother of a trick. That's the whole song, and it is a song about God. Bhakti has a name for this kind of love: vatsalya, the tenderness of a parent for a child. Instead of looking up at God from far below, the singer stands where Yashoda stands and looks down, at someone small enough to worry about. And it's still how many Hindus pray. In many homes, a small image of baby Krishna, Laddu Gopal, is bathed, dressed, fed and put to bed like a child. In Vallabha's tradition, Surdas's songs are sung to Krishna as part of that daily care.
screen: `WHY WHINE? SING HIS PLAY.` · `THE SURSAGAR: THE OCEAN OF SUR.` · `MOTHER, WHEN WILL MY BRAID GROW?` · then, large: `VATSALYA: LOVING GOD AS YOUR CHILD.`

segments.voice: Notice, without arguing, whatever your mind likes to sing about you: what's wrong, what's late, what isn't enough. Then turn, the way the teacher turned Surdas. If you keep a small shrine, look at the image there the way Yashoda looks at a boy with a short braid, and offer it something small: a sip of water, a sweet, a line of song. If you don't pray, turn toward someone small in your care and hold them with a little worry and a lot of fondness.
Surdas. A singer of Braj who, tradition says, was blind, and who turned from his own sorrow to sing of a child named Krishna.
screen: `SURDAS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: vatsalya, loving God as your own child. The sad song about yourself can make room for someone small. Tomorrow: what does a boy with butter on his face tell his mother?

928.title: The butter thief's defense
928.hook: a small boy with butter on his face makes his case
928.carry: lila: God comes close enough to be scolded
928.tomorrow: what happens when a scholar comes to teach the cowherd girls?
928.howItsDone: Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo is sung as a bhajan in homes and temples, and around Krishna's birthday, Janmashtami, children sometimes act out the butter thief's story.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Surdas turned from his own sorrow to a little boy asking when his braid would grow. Vatsalya: loving God as your own child.
screen: `SURDAS.` · `VATSALYA.`

segments.voice: The complaint comes from the neighbors. Butter is missing from their houses again. Pots are cracked. There are small handprints. So the accused is brought before his mother, and the song lets us see his face, still shiny with butter. He doesn't cry or run. He opens his mouth and begins his defense. It's one of the songs carried under the name of Surdas, and it plays like a tiny courtroom: one small boy, no lawyer, and an argument he has clearly been working on.
screen: `THE NEIGHBORS COMPLAIN.` → `BUTTER ON HIS FACE.` → `THE DEFENSE BEGINS.`

segments.voice: It opens with the line the whole song hangs on. Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo. Mother, I didn't eat the butter. Then the case, point by point. One: at dawn you sent me off behind the cows, and I wandered the forest all day. When would I have had time? Two: look at these arms. I'm a child. How could I reach a pot hung up high? Three: the cowherd boys have it in for me. They smeared it on my face themselves. Then he changes tactics and gets hurt. Mother, you're too trusting, you believe whatever they say. Maybe you think I'm somebody else's child. And the big finish: here, take back my stick and my blanket. I quit. You've made me dance enough. The song ends: Surdas says, then Yashoda smiled, and pulled him close against her heart. Case closed. The Bhagavata told how the butter thief stole; Surdas adds the defense, and gives the last word to a mother's smile. Here's the teaching under the joke. Hindus call Krishna's childhood his lila, his play: the Lord of everything comes small enough to be caught, scolded and hugged. Many teachers read the butter as the devotee's heart, the thing he really comes to steal. That's why he's lovingly called Makhan Chor, the butter thief, why families offer him butter and sugar on Janmashtami, his birthday, and why teams in Maharashtra build human pyramids to break a pot of curd hung up high.
screen: `MOTHER, I DIDN'T EAT THE BUTTER.` · `DAWN, SMALL ARMS, JEALOUS FRIENDS.` · `YASHODA SMILED AND PULLED HIM CLOSE.` · then, large: `LILA: GOD CLOSE ENOUGH TO SCOLD.`

segments.voice: Picture the yard: the neighbors, the cracked pot, a small boy with butter on his face making his case, and Yashoda's mouth starting to twitch. If you pray, offer Krishna something small and sweet in your mind, the way families offer butter and sugar on his birthday, and be glad that God came close enough to be scolded. If you don't pray, bring to mind someone who argues their way out around you, and let the smile arrive before the ruling.
Surdas. The singer who let a small boy argue his case, and gave the last line to his mother's smile.

929.title: The gopis answer Uddhava
929.hook: a learned messenger comes to teach the gopis, and a bee gets an earful
929.carry: bhakti: our one mind went with Shyam
929.tomorrow: what does a princess do with a cup of poison?
929.howItsDone: Bhramargit songs from the Sursagar are sung in Krishna devotion, and the meeting of Uddhava and the gopis is retold in kirtan, dance and Ras Lila performances in the Braj region.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Surdas let a boy with butter on his face argue his case. Lila: God comes close enough to be scolded.
screen: `SURDAS.` · `LILA: GOD CLOSE ENOUGH TO SCOLD.`

segments.voice: Krishna has gone. He grew up, left for the city of Mathura, and didn't come back. In Braj, the cowherd girls, the gopis, are still waiting at the edge of the village. Then a chariot comes down the road, and it isn't him. It's his friend Uddhava, a learned man, with a message. Krishna is everywhere, he tells them. Stop grieving for a body. Close your eyes, practice yoga, meditate on the one without form. He has come to teach them. He hasn't come expecting to be taught.
screen: `KRISHNA HAS GONE TO THE CITY.` → `A CHARIOT, BUT NOT HIM.` → `UDDHAVA BRINGS A LESSON.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata tells this scene, and in it one of the gopis, deep in sorrow, starts talking to a bee that has landed near her, scolding it as if it were Krishna's go-between. That little bee became a doorway. The gopis' bee songs are called the bhramargit, and in the Sursagar Surdas fills them with sharp, funny, grieving answers to Uddhava. Here's one. Udho, man na bhaye das bees. Uddhava, we don't have ten or twenty minds. We had one, and it went with Shyam. So who's left here to meditate on your formless one? It's airtight. Uddhava's method needs a mind to sit still. Theirs walked off down the road to Mathura. In other songs they needle him: take your load of yoga back to the city; nobody here is buying. And between the jokes they keep asking the bee: does he remember us? The river, the cows? Two ways toward God meet in this yard: jnana, knowledge of the formless, and bhakti, love for one with a face. Surdas lets the gopis win the argument. The Bhagavata says Uddhava left wishing he could be a creeper or a bush in Braj, just to be touched by the dust of their feet. But the scene doesn't mock him. He brought the highest teaching he knew, and the tradition keeps both roads open, the path of knowing and the path of love. What Surdas adds is love heard from the inside: a heart that has given its whole mind away.
screen: `A GOPI SCOLDS A BEE.` · `WE DON'T HAVE TEN OR TWENTY MINDS.` · `JNANA AND BHAKTI: TWO ROADS.` · then, large: `UDDHAVA WISHES TO BE A CREEPER IN BRAJ.`

930.title: Mira and the cup of poison
930.hook: a cup of poison, and a woman who laughs as she drinks it
930.tomorrow: who does Mira say she belongs to?
930.howItsDone: Mira bhajans are sung in homes, temples and concerts, and her life is retold in plays, films and devotional story sessions.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-THIRTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Surdas's gopis told a learned messenger, we had one mind, and it went with Shyam. Bhakti.
screen: `SURDAS.` · `OUR ONE MIND WENT WITH SHYAM.`

segments.voice: A cup is carried into a woman's room. Inside it, the song says, is poison, sent by the Rana, the head of the royal family she married into. She knows exactly what it is. She drinks it, and she laughs. And the poison, the song says, turned to nectar. That woman is Mirabai, and the remarkable thing is who tells the story. Not a court record. Songs sung in her voice. So who is this woman, singing about a cup of poison?
screen: `A CUP FROM THE RANA.` → `SHE DRINKS, AND LAUGHS.` → `WHO IS SINGING?`

segments.voice: What reaches us of Mira comes mostly through songs sung under her name and stories told about her, and tradition weaves the two together. Tradition says she was a Rajput princess who loved Krishna from girlhood. One story: a wandering holy man gave the child a small image of Krishna, and she wouldn't let it go. Another: watching a wedding procession, she asked her mother who her own bridegroom would be, and her mother, half joking, pointed to Krishna. Mira took her at her word. Married into the royal house of Mewar, she kept singing and dancing in the temple among wandering sadhus, and her husband's family took it as a disgrace. The songs tell of attempts to stop her: the cup of poison, and a basket said to hold a snake that, when she opened it, was a garland. Through it all she sings to Krishna as Giridhar, the one who lifted the mountain, and calls him her husband, her beloved, the one she belongs to. Some songs in her voice even name Raidas, a saint born into a leatherworking caste, as her guru. A queen bowing to a cobbler: that's the teaching. In bhakti, love of God outranks birth, caste and rank, and saints from every kind of family stand side by side. Other singers have sung in Mira's voice too, and some readers ask which songs go back to her. What reaches us is still a clear voice: a woman who knows whose she is.
screen: `SONGS AND STORIES, WOVEN TOGETHER.` · `POISON, AND A SNAKE THAT WAS A GARLAND.` · `A QUEEN WHO BOWED TO RAIDAS.` · then, large: `IN BHAKTI, LOVE OUTRANKS BIRTH.`

931.hook: mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else
931.carry: belonging to God loosens the world's shame
931.tomorrow: how can a woman who left a palace call herself rich?
931.howItsDone: Mere to Giridhar Gopal is sung as a bhajan in homes, temples and concerts, often in a simple call-and-response that lets anyone join the refrain.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: in Mirabai's songs, a queen kept singing among wandering sadhus, though the Rana sent poison. In bhakti, love outranks birth.
screen: `MIRABAI'S SONGS.` · `LOVE OUTRANKS BIRTH.`

segments.voice: Some songs argue. Some plead. This one simply states a fact, the way you'd give someone your address. Mere to Giridhar Gopal, doosro na koi. Mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else. It's one of the songs sung in Mira's voice, short enough to carry in your pocket. And it closes a week of singers who each found a way to belong.
screen: `SOME SONGS ARGUE.` → `THIS ONE STATES A FACT.` → `MINE IS GIRIDHAR GOPAL.`

segments.voice: Mine is Giridhar Gopal, the mountain-lifter, the cowherd, and no one else. The one who wears the peacock-feather crown, he is my husband. That word, husband, is the scandal and the point. Bhakti poets often picture the soul as a bride and God as the beloved; Mira sings it as her life. Tradition says she was married to a prince. In the song, she says plainly that she belongs to someone else. Then she counts the cost. Father, mother, brothers, relatives: she has let them go. Sitting among the holy ones, she says, I've lost lok laj, the world's sense of shame. What can anyone do to me now? Then an image that's hard to forget. With my tears, again and again, I watered the vine of love. Now it has spread, and it bears its fruit of joy. Notice the order. Not: I belong to no one, so I'm free. The reverse: I belong so completely to one that the world's opinion has lost its grip. That's a logic of bhakti, folded into one song. Now the week. Bhakti teachers name several moods of love for God. Tulsidas gave Hanuman's song, a servant's love. Surdas stood in Yashoda's yard with a parent's love, and gave the gopis their answer: our one mind went with Shyam. And Mira, a bride's love: mine is Giridhar. Three singers, one shape. Each belongs to someone, and the belonging sets the song free.
screen: `HE IS MY HUSBAND.` · `I'VE LOST THE WORLD'S SHAME.` · `TEARS WATERED THE VINE OF LOVE.` · then, large: `THREE SINGERS, ONE SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Let the breath come and go slowly, like water poured on a young vine, and ask one plain question: whose am I? Not what do I do, but whose: a person, a community, God, a promise you keep. Let the answer come in your own words or none, notice whether some opinion out there has a little less grip on you, and if you pray, rest in the one you belong to.
Mirabai's songs. Mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else: belonging so complete that the world's shame lost its hold.
